intro: Read the deck for the content and these notes for the thinking. The note under each slide explains it, gives you something to remember and warns where people slip. Work each worked example in pencil first. Then close the page and answer the recall questions from memory, and keep a draft logframe of your own beside you.

sections.title: What a Logframe Is
sections.big_idea: A logframe is a **one-page matrix** that answers four questions: what you are achieving, how you will know, where the proof comes from, and what must hold.
in_plain_words: The matrix has four levels of result down the left side: impact, outcome, outputs, and activities with inputs. Three columns sit beside them: indicators, means of verification and assumptions. Read down the first column to test the logic, and read across a row to test whether the result can be measured.

The logframe began at USAID in 1969 and is now a near-universal donor requirement, written in many vocabularies. It is a summary that stands in for none of the theory of change, work plan, budget, risk log or M&E plan. **Build the theory of change first**, then compress its causal spine into the grid.

key_terms.meaning: A one-page matrix of results, indicators, sources and assumptions.
Reading the left column to test whether the results chain holds.
Reading across a row to test measurement and verification.
A narrative and diagram of how and why change happens.
A hierarchy of objectives, good for portfolios and strategy.

worked_example.title: Sort four statements
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A reviewer asks you to place each statement in the right column of a logframe.
steps: We will see 1,500 farmers trained: this is a result, so it goes in the left column.
The number of farmers trained, from 0 to 1,500: this is an indicator.
Training registers kept by the M&E officer: this is the means of verification.
Farmers' fields get enough water: this is an assumption, an external condition.
worked_example.answer: Results, indicators, means of verification and assumptions, one statement per column.

mistakes: Treating the logframe as the whole plan. It summarises five other documents and replaces none.
Reading it only down the left column, which gives a plan with no monitoring.
Assuming purpose, outcome and specific objective differ. They can name the same row in different formats.

recall.q: What four questions does the matrix answer?
recall.a: What are we trying to achieve, how will we know, where does the proof come from, and what must hold.

recall.q: Who developed the logframe and when?
recall.a: Leon Rosenberg and colleagues at USAID, in 1969.

recall.q: What is the commonest empty answer in a logframe?
recall.a: Where the proof comes from. Indicators get written without checking the data can be obtained.

recall.q: Which tool should you build first?
recall.a: The theory of change, then summarise its causal spine into the logframe.

recall.q: What is the weakness of a logframe, per the family table?
recall.a: It compresses the detail and implies linearity.

sections.title: The Results Chain
sections.big_idea: Everything hangs on the chain from inputs to impact, and the commonest fault is **placing a result one level too high**.
in_plain_words: The chain runs inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, impact, with one-word tests: spent, done, delivered, changed, contributed to. Inputs, activities and outputs are within your control and you are accountable for them. Outcomes you influence, and impact you only contribute to.

Each step upward is an if–then hypothesis, and the risk rises as you climb. The step from outputs to outcome, where others must take up what you delivered, is where most projects fail. **Claim contribution and share the credit** for outcomes and impact. Design from the top down, and deliver from the bottom up.

key_terms.meaning: The goods and services you deliver, complete on delivery.
A change in others' behaviour, knowledge or condition.
The widening distance between what a project delivers and the change it hopes for.
A plausible link to a change that has many causes.
A claim that one level will produce the next, which can fail.

worked_example.title: Place four statements
worked_example.setup: Use the output-or-outcome test: could you report it complete the day you finish delivery?
steps: 500 health workers trained: you can tick it off yourself, so it is an output.
Health workers correctly manage cases: others must change practice, so it is an outcome.
Child mortality falls: many causes and a long horizon, so it is impact.
Training curriculum developed: a deliverable and no change in others, so it is an output.

mistakes: Describing an output in outcome grammar, such as improved capacity of 500 health workers.
Promising an outcome as if you controlled it.
Designing bottom-up from what you already do and calling the result an outcome.

recall.q: What are the one-word tests for the five links?
recall.a: Spent, done, delivered, changed, contributed to.

recall.q: Which levels are in your control?
recall.a: Inputs, activities and outputs.

recall.q: Where do most projects fail in the chain?
recall.a: The step from outputs to outcome, where people must take up what was delivered.

recall.q: How should you phrase claims about impact?
recall.a: As contribution, since the project is one of several forces.

recall.q: Why is secondary-school completion hard to observe in the girls' education example?
recall.a: A three-year project cannot observe completion for girls enrolling in year one.

sections.title: Inputs, Activities, Outputs
sections.big_idea: The bottom half of the matrix is **within your control**, so write it as specific, countable, costable deliverables.
in_plain_words: Inputs are resources the project consumes, specific enough to cost, including partner and community contributions. Activities are verbs that convert inputs into outputs. Outputs are completed deliverables with a number, such as 1,500 farmers trained in drip irrigation. Phrase each level in its own grammar.

Keep one result per box, and keep the matrix small: one impact, one outcome and four to six outputs. Test the left column upward: is this enough to plausibly produce the level above? **Build the matrix block by block**, tie inputs to the budget, and budget the verification work.

levels.label: Outputs
levels.sub: a number and a completed verb

diagram.caption: the controllable half, top to bottom

key_terms.meaning: A resource a project consumes: money, staff time, equipment, partner contributions.
A manageable set of activities, say 3 to 6 per output.
A statement with and in it often hides two results.
Budget divided by the output indicator, which traceability makes possible.
The place for the detailed task list that the matrix leaves out.

worked_example.title: Cost per output
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A club programme budgets 24,00,000 rupees for 800 girls enrolled in 40 clubs.
steps: Cost per participant: 2,400,000 ÷ 800 = 3,000 rupees.
Girls per club: 800 ÷ 40 = 20.
Check the block: the output is countable, each activity traces to it and the inputs match a budget line.
Ask whether the output is worth its share of the cost against its contribution to the outcome.
worked_example.answer: The programme costs 3,000 rupees per girl and has 20 girls per club.

mistakes: Writing activities as capacity building or awareness raising, which cannot be scheduled or costed.
Leaving out participants' time and government counterpart effort when costing inputs.
Listing ten outputs in a one-page summary. You probably have two projects or a work plan.

recall.q: What two things should an output statement contain?
recall.a: A number and a completed verb.

recall.q: What grammar fits each level?
recall.a: Activities an infinitive verb, outputs a past participle with a number, outcomes a present-tense change in others.

recall.q: What does an and in a result usually mean?
recall.a: Two results hiding in one box.

recall.q: What is the usual target size of a matrix?
recall.a: One impact, one outcome and four to six outputs.

recall.q: What does the vertical test ask?
recall.a: At each step, is this enough to plausibly produce the level above?

sections.title: Outcomes & Impact
sections.big_idea: The outcome is **the change you are really after**, the uptake of your outputs, and the impact is the higher purpose you only contribute to.
in_plain_words: An outcome is a change in behaviour, knowledge, relationships or condition among named others. It is usually the project's purpose, and the hardest row to write well. Run five tests: someone else is the subject, it is reachable, it is measurable, it is one thing, and it is worth doing.

Impact is the long-term change you contribute to, shared with other actors and beyond the project horizon. The output-to-outcome gap needs the assumptions column or an extra output. Outcomes take time to appear, so **budget the follow-up round at design**. Sustainability asks who pays, maintains and keeps capacity after you leave.

key_terms.meaning: Another name for the outcome row in some formats.
Another name for impact.
The leap where delivered goods may not be taken up.
Honest impact wording that avoids claiming sole causation.
Whether change lasts after funding ends.

worked_example.title: Test an outcome
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A draft outcome says: smallholder farmers in 40 villages adopt and sustain drip irrigation. The project trains 1,500 farmers and expects 60 per cent still using drip at 12 months.
steps: Is the subject someone else? Yes, the farmers, and the target group is named.
Is it one thing and measurable? Yes, adoption can be counted at a follow-up.
Expected farmers still using drip: 1,500 × 60 ÷ 100 = 900.
The word sustain needs a follow-up survey, so the budget must include it.
worked_example.answer: The outcome passes the tests, with 900 farmers still using drip if the target is met.

mistakes: Writing an outcome about the project team. The subject must be someone else.
Writing three outcomes to satisfy every stakeholder. That is often three projects.
Promising an impact target dated inside the project period.

recall.q: What is the output–outcome gap?
recall.a: The leap from deliverables to others' uptake, where assumptions matter most.

recall.q: Which five tests apply to an outcome statement?
recall.a: Is the subject someone else, is it reachable, is it measurable, is it one thing, is it worth doing.

recall.q: Why do most logframes allow one outcome?
recall.a: Focus: a project chasing three outcomes usually does none well.

recall.q: Name the five needs of behaviour change.
recall.a: Knowing what to do, being able to, wanting to, a reminder or trigger, and it working the first time.

recall.q: What is the strongest form of sustainability?
recall.a: A practice that benefits the adopter enough to continue without outside support.

sections.title: Indicators
sections.big_idea: An indicator is a **specific, measurable sign** that a result has been achieved, and a full one has a unit, baseline, target and date.
in_plain_words: For each result you name at least one indicator that would move if the result were real. Objectively verifiable means two people measuring independently get the same answer. Make indicators SMART, and test each by asking what value it takes if the project succeeds and what value if it fails.

Quantitative indicators count; qualitative ones need a defined method. A proxy needs its claim stated, because of Goodhart's law. One or two indicators per result are usually enough. **Borrow standard definitions** from sources such as SDG indicators, DHS or NFHS to gain a free benchmark.

diagram.note: an indicator with no baseline is the commonest logframe fault

key_terms.meaning: Objectively verifiable indicator.
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.
The value at the start, without which change cannot be shown.
Splitting a figure by sex, age, caste, location or disability.
A stand-in for a result with no direct meter.

worked_example.title: Make a target concrete
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. An indicator reads: percentage of trained midwives correctly performing newborn resuscitation, rising from 40% to 80% by end of year 2. The project trains 150 midwives.
steps: Baseline count: 150 × 40 ÷ 100 = 60 midwives.
Target count: 150 × 80 ÷ 100 = 120 midwives.
Extra midwives needed: 120 − 60 = 60.
The date and unit are present. Add disaggregation and an observation method.
worked_example.answer: The target means 60 more midwives performing correctly, from 60 to 120.

mistakes: Leaving baselines as TBD, which usually stay undetermined.
Choosing an indicator that measures your activity instead of the change.
Adding indicators with no named collector, frequency or decision.

recall.q: What are the parts of a full indicator?
recall.a: Unit, baseline, target, date and disaggregation.

recall.q: What is Goodhart's law?
recall.a: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

recall.q: Why test an indicator against success and failure values?
recall.a: If the two are close, the indicator does not discriminate, so replace it.

recall.q: Which SMART element is caught least well?
recall.a: Relevance, because an indicator can be perfect on the other four and measure the wrong thing.

recall.q: How many indicators per result are usually enough?
recall.a: One or two.

sections.title: Means of Verification
sections.big_idea: The MoV says **how you will actually get the number**, and it is the budget test for the whole matrix.
in_plain_words: A good entry names the source, method, frequency and responsible person. Project records suit outputs, surveys suit outcomes, observation suits practice, and official statistics suit impact and context. Courtesy bias is the weakness of surveying your own participants, so use independent enumerators where the claim matters.

If you cannot pay to verify a result, you cannot claim it. Options are to change the indicator, reduce frequency or sample, use an existing survey such as NFHS or PLFS, or drop the claim. Keep raw data and the same tool across baseline and endline. **Columns two and three are in effect your monitoring plan.**

diagram.caption: cost rises as you move up the chain

key_terms.meaning: Means of verification: the source, method, frequency and person for each indicator.
Participants reporting more benefit to the organisation that helped them.
A person who collects survey data.
Checking self-reported data against other sources.
A one-page sheet holding definitions and formulas.

worked_example.title: The monitoring budget
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A project costs 2,00,00,000 rupees, and the deck suggests monitoring often takes 5 to 10 per cent of project cost. An endline panel survey is quoted at 25,00,000 rupees.
steps: The quote of 2,500,000 is above even the upper end.
Choose an option: reduce the sample, survey at endline only, or align to NFHS or PLFS.
worked_example.answer: A monitoring budget of 10 to 20 lakh rupees cannot pay for a 25 lakh survey, so change the design.

mistakes: Writing project records as a source without naming which record, who keeps it and who checks it.
Changing the measurement tool between baseline and endline without running both once.
Surveying outcomes so often that measurement disrupts the work.

recall.q: What four things must an MoV entry name?
recall.a: The source, method, frequency and responsible person.

recall.q: What is courtesy bias?
recall.a: Participants surveyed by the organisation that gave them something report more benefit than they would to a third party.

recall.q: What are the options when verification is unaffordable?
recall.a: Change the indicator, reduce the frequency, reduce the sample, use an existing survey, or drop the claim.

recall.q: Why is aligning to a national survey underused?
recall.a: It costs nothing, gives a comparison for free, and produces a trusted figure, yet teams forget it.

recall.q: What does a fuller M&E plan add to columns two and three?
recall.a: Tools, sampling, responsibilities, timing, analysis and use.

sections.title: Assumptions
sections.big_idea: Assumptions are the **external conditions** that must hold for each step, and every good one comes with something you can observe.
in_plain_words: Assumptions are the and also behind every if–then. A real assumption is outside your control, necessary for the step above, specific enough to monitor and uncertain. Place them on the arrows. The output-to-outcome arrow should carry the most, because it is the step you control least.

Sort each assumption by how likely it is to hold and how important it is. Almost certain ones are dropped, uncertain and important ones are monitored, and unlikely and important ones are killers that call for redesign. **Anything you can influence belongs in an output or activity**, and the column is no disclaimer. Revisit it at every review.

key_terms.meaning: An external condition that must hold for a step in the logic to work.
One that is both essential and unlikely to hold.
A sign you can check to see whether an assumption holds.
If outputs are delivered and assumptions hold, then the outcome is reached.
A matrix whose assumptions are things the project could have done.

worked_example.title: Sort four assumptions
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Sort each assumption for a drip-irrigation project by likelihood and importance.
steps: Rainfall is within the normal range: uncertain and important, so keep it and monitor IMD seasonal data.
Trained staff are not transferred this year: likely but not sure, so keep it and check HR records quarterly.
The government will pass a required policy that is very unlikely to pass: unlikely and essential, a killer.
Farmers have the sun: almost certain, so drop it.
worked_example.answer: Keep two with monitoring, flag one killer for redesign, and drop one.

mistakes: Putting partner capacity in the assumptions column. It belongs in an output.
Writing assumptions too vague to observe, which records an excuse in advance.
Discovering a killer assumption at mid-term, which costs a year and a reputation.

recall.q: What are the four tests of a real assumption?
recall.a: Outside your control, necessary for the step, specific enough to monitor, and uncertain.

recall.q: Where should assumptions sit?
recall.a: On the arrows between levels, with the boxes left clear.

recall.q: What is a killer assumption?
recall.a: One that is both essential and unlikely to hold.

recall.q: Which arrow should carry the most assumptions?
recall.a: Output to outcome.

recall.q: What should you do about a killer assumption?
recall.a: State it in the proposal with the mitigation, and redesign or say so before signing.

sections.title: Risk
sections.big_idea: A risk is an assumption that might fail, and a log gives each one **a score, a response, an owner and a trigger**.
in_plain_words: Flip an assumption and you have a risk: rainfall is normal becomes drought reduces yields. The matrix is for the funder and the risk log is for the manager. Score each risk by likelihood and impact on a 1 to 5 scale, and treat the product as a rough sort.

Respond with one of four Ts: treat, transfer, tolerate or terminate. Categories are contextual, programmatic, institutional or fiduciary, and reputational and safeguarding. Safeguarding risk can only be treated or terminated. **Every risk needs an owner and an observable trigger**, and the log is reviewed on a schedule, with changes logged.

spokes.label: Tolerate
spokes.sub: monitor and keep a plan B

key_terms.meaning: A scored, owned list of risks with responses and review dates.
A 1 to 5 score on each axis, multiplied for a rough priority.
The observable sign that a risk is materialising.
The risk that a project harms the people it serves.
The response prepared for a tolerated risk.

worked_example.title: Score three risks
worked_example.setup: Use the scores from the worked risk row: drought 3 by 4, staff transfer 4 by 3, weak partner financial controls 2 by 5. Add a trigger for enrolment.
steps: Drought: 3 × 4 = 12.
Staff transfer: 4 × 3 = 12.
Partner controls: 2 × 5 = 10.
Two risks tie, so discuss which sits in the high–high corner and assign an owner to each.
A trigger for 500 expected enrolments: below 60 per cent by month 3, so 500 × 60 ÷ 100 = 300.
worked_example.answer: Scores 12, 12 and 10, with a trigger at 300 enrolments by month 3.

mistakes: Scoring risks and then treating the product as a precise measurement.
Passing delivery risk to a local partner without the resources to manage it.
Writing the risk log once and filing it.

recall.q: What are the four Ts?
recall.a: Treat, transfer, tolerate, terminate.

recall.q: What does a risk entry need to be operational?
recall.a: An owner, a trigger, a response and a review date.

recall.q: Which risk category cannot be tolerated?
recall.a: Safeguarding: it can only be treated or terminated.

recall.q: What does tolerating require?
recall.a: A named trigger and a plan B.

recall.q: When should the risk log be reviewed?
recall.a: At every board or quarterly review, and after an incident.

sections.title: Building the Matrix
sections.big_idea: Build in the right sequence, with people in a room, and test the result in **two directions**: vertical logic and horizontal logic.
in_plain_words: The order of work is theory of change, left column, assumptions, indicators and means of verification. Starting with indicators feels concrete and measures whatever the team already does. The ZOPP tradition builds the matrix in a workshop, which makes it weaker on paper and stronger in practice.

Vertical logic asks whether each level plus its assumptions is sufficient for the next. Horizontal logic reads each row across: does the indicator measure the result, can the MoV supply it, is the assumption external? Revise the logframe at agreed review points and **log every change with a date and a reason**.

key_terms.meaning: GTZ's participatory, objectives-oriented planning method, built in a workshop.
Whether the level below, with its assumptions, is enough for the next.
A row whose four parts no longer describe the same thing.
A review point where activities and assumptions often change.
One authoritative version mapped to each funder's format.

worked_example.title: Read one row across
worked_example.setup: The full example row: outcome farmers adopt and sustain drip irrigation; indicator 60% of trained farmers still using drip at 12 months; MoV a follow-up survey of 300 farmers in year 2.
steps: Result to indicator: it measures use at 12 months, so it measures the result.
Indicator to MoV: can a sample of 300 supply a percentage? Yes.
Expected count if the target is met: 300 × 60 ÷ 100 = 180 farmers using drip.
MoV to assumption: water availability and crop prices are about the world, and they are external and monitorable.
worked_example.answer: The row passes the horizontal test, and about 180 of 300 sampled farmers should be using drip.

mistakes: Starting with indicators because they feel concrete.
Reviewing the matrix only yourself. Familiarity hides gaps.
Treating the matrix as fixed when most donors allow revision at review points.

recall.q: What is the build order?
recall.a: Theory of change, left column, assumptions, indicators, means of verification.

recall.q: What does vertical logic test?
recall.a: The theory: whether each level is enough to produce the next.

recall.q: What does horizontal logic test?
recall.a: The measurement: indicator, MoV and assumption in each row.

recall.q: What are common faults reviewers find?
recall.a: Results at the wrong level, no baselines, too many outcomes, assumptions that are excuses, and unaffordable MoV.

recall.q: Why log revisions?
recall.a: Logged revision looks like management, and unlogged revision looks like moving the goalposts.

sections.title: Critiques & Limits
sections.big_idea: The logframe has four serious critiques, and most are about **how the tool is used**, which is where your response lies.
in_plain_words: Change is rarely linear, so the chain handles feedback loops and emergent effects poorly. The matrix rewards the measurable, so teams drift toward counting outputs. Treated as a contract, it locks in a plan that should flex. And it is written upward in the donor's language.

Responses are practical: pair the logframe with outcome harvesting or developmental evaluation for complex problems, include one uncomfortable outcome indicator, schedule revisions, and build the logic with participants. **Alternatives are companions**: Outcome Mapping, Outcome Harvesting, Most Significant Change and contribution analysis. Hold the logframe lightly.

diagram.caption: each critique with its practical response

key_terms.meaning: Changing the plan as learning arrives, within agreed review points.
Suits change that runs through many actors' behaviour.
Works backwards from outcomes that could not be predicted.
Participant-defined, story-based evidence.
A method for cases where attribution is impossible.

worked_example.title: Match critique to remedy
worked_example.setup: Match each problem to the response suggested in the deck.
steps: A governance project has feedback loops and unplanned effects: pair the logframe with outcome harvesting or developmental evaluation.
A team reports only people trained and meetings held: add one outcome indicator that would be uncomfortable if it did not move.
A team is penalised for dropping a failing output: agree a stop-or-change rule and a revision protocol at inception.
The logic reflects only donor categories: build it with participants and add downward reporting.
worked_example.answer: Four critiques, four remedies, and most remedies concern how the tool is used.

mistakes: Rejecting the logframe because of the critiques. The aim is to keep the discipline and avoid the traps.
Treating a logframe as complete evidence of change in a complex setting.
Agreeing targets before the baseline exists.

recall.q: What are the four critiques?
recall.a: Change is not linear, it crowds out the uncountable, it locks in the plan, and it serves the donor.

recall.q: What drift does the second critique describe?
recall.a: Teams drift toward what is easy to count, such as outputs and numbers trained.

recall.q: When is linearity a reasonable approximation?
recall.a: For a service-delivery project with a well-understood mechanism.

recall.q: What is the practical pattern with alternatives?
recall.a: A logframe for accountability and one alternative for learning, feeding revisions back.

recall.q: Which course does the deck cite on the donor-power critique?
recall.a: Decolonial Development 101.

sections.title: Tools & Practice
sections.big_idea: Funders ask for slightly different formats, and **one master matrix** in your own vocabulary can be mapped to all of them.
in_plain_words: The EU, FCDO, USAID, UN agencies and GIZ each use their own names and add their own asks, such as annual milestones from FCDO. Most logframes live in spreadsheets, with Word for the annex and M&E platforms for live tracking. Keep one authoritative copy with a version and date.

A reusable column checklist and a ten-minute reviewer's test catch most problems. If the first test fails, fix the logic before anything else. The fastest way to learn is to draft one for a project you know and have a colleague attack it. **Say the whole tool in one sentence**: the change you bet on, how you will know, the proof, and what must hold.

key_terms.meaning: An annual target per indicator, asked for by FCDO.
One version in your own vocabulary, mapped to each format.
Five questions a reviewer asks to check a matrix quickly.
The one-page sheet where indicator definitions live.
Keeping one authoritative copy with a number and a date.

worked_example.title: Run the ten-minute test
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A draft matrix has three outcomes, two baselines marked TBD, an assumption that partner staff will be trained, and a left column that needs explaining at each jump.
steps: Does the left column read as a story? No, so the logic fails first.
Is there exactly one clear outcome? No, there are three.
Does every indicator have a baseline and a source? No, two say TBD.
Are the assumptions external? No, training partner staff is the project's own job and belongs in an output.
worked_example.answer: Fail on four tests. Fix the logic first, because it cannot be repaired at the indicator column.

mistakes: Maintaining several funder versions independently, which lets them diverge.
Fixing the lower tests before the first when the logic does not read.
Choosing expensive software to rescue a muddled matrix.

recall.q: What distinctive ask does FCDO make?
recall.a: Annual milestones per indicator and a separate theory of change.

recall.q: What does USAID ask for besides the matrix?
recall.a: A results framework plus an activity MEL plan.

recall.q: What are the five questions in the ten-minute test?
recall.a: Story-like left column, exactly one outcome, baselines and sources, external assumptions with killers flagged, and agreement with the budget and work plan.

recall.q: Why draft a logframe for a project you know?
recall.a: Drafting for an unfamiliar project teaches the format, while drafting for your own teaches the logic.

recall.q: What is the one-sentence logframe?
recall.a: The change you bet on, how you will know, where the proof comes from, and what must hold for the bet to pay.

notes.2: Use the agenda to see the logframe as a build order. Sections one to four set out the left column, from the chain through inputs, outputs, outcomes and impact. Five to eight add indicators, verification, assumptions and risk. Nine to eleven assemble, critique and apply the matrix.
notes.4: Treat the four columns as four questions: what are we achieving, how will we know, where does the proof come from, and what must hold. A row that cannot answer one of them is unfinished. The third is the commonest gap, because indicators get written without checking that the data can be obtained.
notes.5: Learn to read the grid two ways. Down the left column you test whether the logic holds, and across a row you test whether the result can be measured and verified. A matrix that reads well down and badly across is a plan with no monitoring. Section 9 turns the two readings into tests.
notes.6: Knowing the history helps you switch between funders. Each donor variant carries its own vocabulary, so purpose, outcome and specific objective can mean the same row in three formats. Before comparing two logframes, map the terms first, since most confusion in a review concerns words and leaves the design untouched.
notes.7: Each benefit has a condition, and the conditions are where logframes fail. A testable theory needs the logic to be challenged, shared language needs agreement on which row is which, and a monitoring spine needs a realistic MoV column. The most valuable hour is the one spent attacking the vertical logic.
notes.8: Keep the logframe in its place. It summarises the theory of change, work plan, budget, risk log and M&E plan, and it replaces none of them. If all five exist and disagree with the logframe, the logframe is wrong, because summaries drift. A tidy grid over a weak theory is wishful thinking.
notes.9: Treat the three tools as complements. The theory of change explains how and why, the results framework shows what sits under what, and the logframe is compact, measurable and donor-ready. Build the theory of change first, then compress its causal spine into the matrix, even if the funder asks only for a logframe.
notes.11: Memorise the chain with its one-word tests: spent, done, delivered, changed, contributed to. The commonest fault is placing a result one level too high. The reason is incentive: calling an output an outcome makes the project look ambitious, and nobody is penalised for it at proposal stage.
notes.12: Separate what you control from what you influence. You are accountable for inputs, activities and outputs, and you influence outcomes and only contribute to impact, which lies beyond your influence. The commonest error is promising an outcome as if it were an output. This framing explains to a funder why you commit to output targets and only contribute to impact.
notes.13: Read upward and every level becomes an if–then bet. The risk rises as you climb. The first two steps usually hold with good management, and the step from outputs to outcome, where people must take up what you delivered, is where most projects fail. An empty assumption there means the logframe is unfinished.
notes.14: Design from the top and deliver from the bottom. Starting at the impact makes every activity earn its place by pointing at a result above it. The standard error is the reverse: starting from what you already do and calling whatever it produces the outcome. If your outcome restates your activities, the logic was never challenged.
notes.15: Follow the girls' education example from impact down to input. Notice the jump from tutored girls (output) to girls completing secondary school (outcome), where families, schools and the economy must cooperate. Ask who has to act at each level, and notice the timing problem: completion cannot be seen within a three-year project.
notes.16: Use the quick test: could you report this complete the day you finish delivery? If yes, it is an output. If someone else must change, it is an outcome. Watch for outputs written in outcome grammar, such as improved capacity of 500 health workers. A training course is a deliverable, and capacity is a change in them.
notes.17: Attribution weakens as you climb. At output level your project is the cause, at outcome level one of several forces, and at impact one contributor among many. Claim contribution for outcomes and impact. If a funder needs an impact attribution claim, that needs a comparison group decided at the start, and no stronger sentence at the end can supply it.
notes.18: This slide points to a diagram of the results chain and the attribution gap in ImpactMojo's The Long View. Look at it before section 3. Keep the picture in mind as you fill in rows, because a logframe is the results chain written as a table.
notes.20: Write inputs specifically enough to cost, such as 12 community mobilisers for 18 months, in place of a vague line like staff. Include partner and community contributions, since they are real inputs. The most forgotten are government counterpart effort and participants' time, and leaving them out makes the project look cheaper than it is.
notes.21: Write activities as specific verbs that can be scheduled and costed. Capacity building, support the ministry and awareness raising fail that test, while train 40 facilitators over 5 days passes. If an activity needs its own sub-plan of ten tasks, it is probably an output in disguise, and the task list belongs in the work plan.
notes.22: An output statement should contain a number and a completed verb, such as 1,500 farmers trained in drip irrigation. If either is missing, the row cannot be monitored. Put quality in the indicator: the percentage passing the practical assessment shows whether the training was worth doing.
notes.23: Use grammar as a diagnostic. Activities take an infinitive verb, outputs a past participle with a number, outcomes a present-tense change in others, and impact a higher-order change. A row in the wrong tense is nearly always at the wrong level. Reading the left column for verb forms is the fastest review pass.
notes.24: Spot the word and in a result statement, because it usually hides two results. Farmers trained and adopting bundles an output with an outcome. Split them so each box carries one result with one indicator. Bundling also hides the take-up assumption that should sit in the fourth column.
notes.25: Keep the matrix small: one impact, one outcome, and four to six outputs. Twelve outputs make a work plan, and forty indicators crowd out delivery. When a stakeholder says but this matters too, point to the work plan or theory of change instead of adding a row.
notes.26: Run the vertical test on the left column: at each step ask whether this is enough to plausibly produce the level above. Gaps mean a missing output, a missing assumption or an over-reaching outcome. Do it aloud with someone who did not write it, before indicators exist, while people still challenge the matrix.
notes.27: Review the matrix in blocks. This block has a countable output (800 girls, 40 clubs), activities traceable to it and inputs that match a budget line. If the four rows are consistent, the block is sound. Building block by block avoids the drift that column-by-column drafting produces.
notes.28: Inputs are the bridge to the budget, so a reader can trace money to activity to output. That makes cost per output possible, and building it in at design is easier than rebuilding from accounting codes later. Budget the M&E work explicitly too, since an unfunded verification column leaves you with output-only monitoring.
notes.29: The bottom half is within your control and mostly discipline. Get outputs countable, activities traceable and inputs tied to the budget, and monitoring almost writes itself. It also gives you the baseline for value-for-money analysis without extra data collection. The riskier half, outcomes, comes next.
notes.31: The outcome is the uptake: what people do differently because of what you delivered. It is the row a funder reads first and the one an evaluation judges, so give it more drafting time than the rest. Write it as a sentence about other people, such as farmers in 40 villages use and maintain drip systems.
notes.32: State the impact you contribute to without claiming to own it. Contributes to reduced child stunting in the district is honest, while reduces stunting alone over-claims. The impact should be shared with other actors and sit beyond the project horizon. If a funder wants an impact target dated inside the project, treat that as a design conversation.
notes.33: Classic discipline allows one purpose. Three outcomes usually mean three projects sharing a budget, and multiple outcomes often hide a lack of decision about what the project is for. Where a programme really has several, use a results framework at programme level with a logframe for each project beneath it.
notes.34: Apply the five tests to a draft outcome before writing any indicator: is the subject someone else, is it reachable from these outputs, can you name the indicator now, is it one thing, and is it worth doing? An outcome that fails the measurable test produces an indicator for something adjacent. The last test matters more than it sounds.
notes.35: This is the output–outcome gap, where projects fail and assumptions matter most. Each right-hand entry, such as no supervision or no supplies, belongs in the assumptions column or in the design. The strongest designs close the gap with an extra output, adding supervision or a supply chain, and skip the hoping.
notes.36: Most outcomes are behaviour change, so check your outputs against the five needs: knowing, being able, wanting, a trigger, and success the first time. Most projects fund only the first and assume the rest. If four of the five are assumptions, the design is a bet on others supplying them.
notes.37: Match measurement timing to the result. Outputs are visible during delivery, outcomes late or after the project, and impact years later. The third row, sustained outcomes 6 to 24 months after, is the one that gets cut. If sustainability is in your outcome statement, budget the follow-up round at design, because it cannot be added once the project ends.
notes.38: Read each row for grammar: contributes to at impact, behaviour change at outcome, a countable deliverable at output. The word sustain in the outcome commits the project to measuring adoption some months after training, which needs a budget line. A commitment with no matching MoV entry is a claim you cannot verify.
notes.39: Sustainability asks who pays, who maintains, whether the behaviour pays the adopter, and whether capacity stays when staff move. The third is the strongest and least common. Where none of the four has an answer, say so plainly: a project that will not outlast its funding can still be worth doing.
notes.40: This recap sets the promises you can make: a target for outputs you control, a credible attempt, measured, for outcomes you influence, and a plausible argued link for impact you contribute to. Being explicit in the proposal is a strength. It also protects the team from an impact target agreed casually.
notes.42: An indicator answers how would we know. Test it by asking what value it takes if the project succeeds and what value if it fails, and replace it if the answers are close. Objectively verifiable means two people measuring independently get the same answer. A target creates an incentive to move the indicator, which differs from moving the result.
notes.43: Use SMART as a checklist and know where it fails. It catches targets nobody can hit and indicators about the wrong thing, and it catches irrelevance least well. An indicator can be specific, measurable and timed while measuring your activity instead of the change. Check relevance deliberately.
notes.44: A full indicator has five parts: a unit, a baseline, a target, a date and disaggregation. Missing baselines are the classic fault: a target without a starting point measures nothing, and baselines marked TBD usually stay undetermined. If you cannot collect a baseline before start-up, name the date and give it an owner.
notes.45: Quantitative indicators answer how much and aggregate easily, though they can miss the mechanism. Qualitative ones answer why and for whom, and need a defined method. A qualitative indicator is legitimate when the MoV names a rubric, scored assessment or case-study protocol. Without one it becomes whatever the report writer says at the end.
notes.46: A proxy stands in for something with no direct meter, such as control over household spending for empowerment. State that it is a proxy and what claim it embeds. Remember Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Attendance and a handwashing station show presence, which differs from learning or practice.
notes.47: Every indicator is a recurring commitment of forms, visits, data entry and cleaning. One or two strong indicators per result are usually enough. Before adding one, ask who will collect it, how often and what decision it will inform. If nothing would change, drop it.
notes.48: Borrow standard definitions where you can: SDG indicators, DHS or NFHS health definitions, WHO handbooks, IRIS+ or sector core sets. You get comparability and a free benchmark, such as a national or state figure to read your result against. It also removes the evaluation argument about whether your bespoke definition was met.
notes.49: Check each worked indicator for unit, baseline, target and date, and note the quality test per level. The middle one matters: an outcome indicator that moves automatically once the output is delivered is measuring the output again. For impact, align to a national survey definition and skip your own survey.
notes.51: The MoV says how you will actually get the number. An entry needs a source, a method, a frequency and a responsible person, and project records alone is no entry. Write the column with the person who will collect the data in the room. They will tell you at once which entries are fantasy.
notes.52: Match each source to its use and weakness. Project records are cheap for outputs but self-reported, surveys suit outcomes but face attrition and courtesy bias, and national data suits context and impact. Courtesy bias is the under-discussed one. Where the outcome claim matters, use independent enumerators at least for the endline.
notes.53: The MoV column is the budget test for the whole matrix. If you cannot pay to verify a result, you cannot claim it, so change the indicator, the frequency, the sample or the claim. The underused option is an existing national survey such as NFHS or PLFS, which costs nothing and offers a trusted comparison.
notes.54: A good entry names method, frequency and person, for example an observation checklist, quarterly, by the M&E officer. Output data is continuous, outcome surveys are periodic, and impact data comes once. Tie frequency to the decision, since annual data cannot correct a delivery problem in month four. Name a real person with time in their workplan.
notes.55: Credibility means a sceptic can follow the MoV to the same conclusion: a reliable source, a consistent method, retained raw data and a traceable chain. The trap is changing the tool between baseline and endline, which destroys the comparison. If you must change it, run both instruments in the changeover round.
notes.56: Read each indicator and its MoV as a pair and ask four things: can this source produce this number, at this frequency, by this person, affordably? Note how cost rises with the level, from cheap records to a before-and-after survey. External enumerators for the outcome survey are a deliberate, costed choice against courtesy bias.
notes.57: Indicators and MoV together are in effect your monitoring plan, and a fuller M&E plan adds definitions, tools, sampling, analysis and use. The last row turns monitoring into management: an indicator with no named user and no decision attached will be collected and filed. For a small project, add a one-page indicator reference sheet.
notes.59: Assumptions are external conditions that must hold for each step, the and also behind every if–then. Test each one on four points: outside your control, necessary, specific enough to monitor, and uncertain. Most columns fail on control or specificity. An assumption you cannot monitor records an excuse in advance.
notes.60: Place assumptions on the arrows and leave the boxes clear, so each one visibly protects a step. The reading is: if we deliver outputs and the assumptions hold, then we reach the outcome. The output-to-outcome arrow should carry the most assumptions because you control it least. An empty entry there is a warning sign.
notes.61: Every good assumption has an observable. Rainfall can be checked against IMD data, a teacher budget against state budget documents, transfers against HR records and prices against a mandi series. Write the observable beside the assumption so a quarterly review can check it, because discovery at evaluation is too late.
notes.62: Run the likelihood and importance sort on every assumption. Almost certain ones are noted and dropped, uncertain and important ones stay and are monitored, and unlikely and important ones are killers that call for redesign, or for stopping if nothing can secure them. Running it takes about twenty minutes and typically empties half the column.
notes.63: A killer assumption is both essential and unlikely to hold. The table gives a response for each: redesign around the current policy, add capacity building as an output, change the intervention, or say so before signing. State the killer in the proposal with its mitigation, since finding it at mid-term costs a year.
notes.64: Assumptions are for external conditions and make a poor place to park what you could act on. Partner capacity belongs in an output, community willingness in an activity, and your own MIS in the MoV column. Reviewers scan the column for things the project could have done, which is the fastest way to spot a defensive matrix.
notes.66: Flip an assumption to its negative and you have a risk: rainfall is normal becomes drought reduces yields. The two columns describe the same uncertainty from different sides, and they have different owners, since the matrix is for the funder and the risk log is for the manager. Keeping both involves no duplication.
notes.67: Score risks by likelihood and impact, each on a 1 to 5 scale, and treat the product as a rough sort and a way to structure conversation. Two teams will differ by several points and both can be reasonable. What matters is a short high–high corner with an owner for each entry. A log where everything is amber has prioritised nothing.
notes.68: Learn the four Ts: treat, transfer, tolerate, terminate. Choosing deliberately matters more than the label. Tolerating needs a named trigger and a plan B. Transfer deserves scrutiny: passing delivery risk to a local partner without the resources to manage it is transfer in name only. Most risks end up treated or tolerated.
notes.69: Cover the four categories: contextual, programmatic, institutional or fiduciary, and reputational and safeguarding. Programmatic is the hardest to write, because it is the risk that your theory of change is wrong. Safeguarding is a standard donor requirement and can only be treated or terminated. Never leave it out.
notes.70: Give every significant risk an owner, a trigger, a response and a review date. The trigger is the element most often missing: a specific, measurable, early sign that the risk is materialising, such as enrolment below 60 per cent of target by month 3. If the drought is bad is no usable trigger.
notes.71: A risk log written once and filed is theatre. Review it at every board or quarterly review, tie the review to the logframe cadence, and log changes in place of overwriting them. After an incident, ask whether it was in the log and, if it was missing, why you did not see it.
notes.72: Read the worked row against the assumption it came from. The assumption says what must hold; the row says what you will do, who does it and when they will know. Each row has a cause and effect, a score, an action, a trigger and a named person. If rows read as concerns, the log is a worry list.
notes.73: This recap puts the pair side by side: the assumptions column names what must hold, and the risk log names what happens if it does not, scores it and assigns a response and owner. With all four columns understood, you are ready to assemble the full matrix and test it as a whole.
notes.75: Follow the build order: theory of change, left column, assumptions, indicators, then means of verification. Each step constrains the next, and assumptions come before indicators because a killer assumption may change the design. Starting with indicators feels concrete and produces a matrix that measures whatever the team was already doing.
notes.76: Build the logframe in a room with delivery staff and, if possible, those it serves. The ZOPP tradition used problem and objective trees with stakeholders. The result is rougher on paper and stronger in practice because the team owns the logic. Even a half-day with field staff surfaces assumptions a desk-written matrix would miss.
notes.77: Test one is the vertical read. At each arrow ask whether the level below, plus its assumptions, is sufficient for the next. Failures mean a missing output, a missing assumption or an over-reach. Hold on to the word sufficiency. If you hear and then a miracle happens, you have found the gap.
notes.78: Test two is the horizontal read: result, indicator, MoV, assumption, as one sentence. Does the indicator measure the result, can the MoV supply it, and is the assumption external? Drift is audible when read aloud and nearly invisible on the page. Vertical tests the theory and horizontal tests the measurement.
notes.79: These five faults account for most review comments: results at the wrong level, no baselines, too many outcomes, assumptions that are excuses, and unaffordable MoV. Run the checks yourself to remove most of the review cycle, and ask a colleague outside the project to repeat them, because familiarity hides gaps.
notes.80: A logframe is a hypothesis, so revise it at agreed review points. Baseline completion, the inception review, mid-term and context shifts each change something different. Log every change with a date and a reason: logged revision looks like management, and unlogged revision looks like moving the goalposts.
notes.81: Read the full row across as a small theory: what changes, how you will know, where the number comes from, and what it depends on. Check result to indicator, indicator to MoV, and MoV to assumption. The water and prices assumption is external, monitorable and material. Use one well-built row as the template for the rest.
notes.83: Learn the four critiques so you can keep the discipline and avoid the traps: change is nonlinear, the matrix crowds out the uncountable, it locks in the plan, and it serves the donor. Notice that three of the four concern how the tool is used and say little about what it is, which is where the response lies.
notes.84: The chain runs one way, so it handles feedback loops poorly and emergent or unintended effects barely at all. For a well-understood service-delivery mechanism, linearity is a reasonable approximation. For governance, norms or systems change, pair the logframe with outcome harvesting or developmental evaluation.
notes.85: Teams drift toward what is easy to count, such as people trained and meetings held, and away from practice changed, decisions shifted and power gained. This is an incentive effect, because teams report against what the matrix asks. The corrective is yours: include at least one outcome indicator that would be uncomfortable if it did not move.
notes.86: A logframe treated as a contract can punish teams for adapting. The fix is revision at agreed review points, logged with reasons, a stated stop-or-change rule, and targets confirmed after the baseline. Adaptive management and a logframe are compatible if revision is scheduled. Agree the protocol with the funder at inception.
notes.87: Logframes are written upward in the donor's categories and language. Partial corrections: build the logic with participants first, add downward reporting and feedback, keep the theory of change alongside, and produce a local-language version. Better logframes do not fully answer this critique, because it asks whom the accountability serves.
notes.88: Treat the alternatives as companions. Outcome Mapping suits change through many actors, Outcome Harvesting suits unpredictable outcomes, Most Significant Change suits participant judgement, and contribution analysis suits cases where attribution is impossible. A common pattern is a logframe for accountability and one of these for learning, feeding revisions back into the matrix.
notes.89: The balanced view is to build the logic first, keep the matrix small, be honest in column four, revise it and hold it lightly. Its failures are mostly failures of use: rigid, upward, as compliance. That is encouraging because use is the part you control. The matrix is a servant and never a master.
notes.91: Funders name the same rows differently: the outcome row is specific objective for the EU, outcome for FCDO and UN agencies, and purpose or IR for USAID. Build one master matrix in your own vocabulary and map it to each format. The FCDO milestone requirement changes the work most, since the trajectory must be planned as well as the endpoint.
notes.92: The tool matters far less than the thinking. A spreadsheet is fine, Word tables suit the proposal annex, and M&E platforms give live tracking at the cost of setup and lock-in. Whatever you use, keep one authoritative copy with a version number and a date, because most confusion is two versions in circulation.
notes.93: Use this as a print-and-check list. Results need one result per row in the right grammar. Indicators need unit, baseline, target, date and disaggregation. MoV needs source, method, frequency and person. Assumptions need to be external and monitored. If any cell is empty or vague, the logframe is unfinished. Run it before anyone else sees the draft.
notes.94: The ten-minute test has five questions: does the left column read as a story, is there one outcome, does every indicator have a baseline and source, are assumptions external with killers flagged, and does it match the budget and work plan? Fix the first failure first, because a matrix whose logic does not read cannot be repaired at the indicator column.
notes.95: Learn by drafting for a project you know well. Start from impact, work down, then fill the other columns and have a colleague attack the logic. Each step teaches something: vague logic, dependence on others, unmeasurable results, unaffordable indicators. The looping back to earlier steps is the process working. Try the Theory of Change Studio first.
notes.96: This slide lists where to go next: Theory of Change 101 for the narrative your logframe summarises, MEL Basics 101 for the wider system, Impact Evaluation 101 and Causal Inference for proving outcomes, Cost Effectiveness 101 for cost per result, and Data Visualization 101 for charts. Pick the one that matches your next gap.
notes.97: Use the reading list by purpose: the EU Project Cycle Management Guidelines and the Bond and FCDO notes for practice, Eyben and colleagues on The Politics of Evidence for the critique, Rogers on complexity and theory-based evaluation, and BetterEvaluation for alternative methods. Read the critique even if you plan to use logframes daily.
notes.98: Say the logframe in one sentence: the change you are betting on, how you will know it happened, where the proof comes from, and what must hold for the bet to pay. If you can say those four sentences about your own project without looking at the matrix, it has done its job. If you cannot, the fix is a conversation.
notes.99: This recap compresses the course into five lines: rows are controlled, influenced and contributed to, indicators carry unit, baseline, target and date, MoV names source, method, frequency and person, and assumptions are external and monitored. Keep the sceptical read: whose logic is this, what has to hold, and who pays to find out?
